title: San Miguel County Wells: Depth, Yield & Drilling Cost
meta_description: San Miguel County wells have a median depth of 182 feet. Compare yields, water levels and estimated finished-well costs of $17,800-$30,200.
h1: Planning a Well in San Miguel County
intro_html:
A well near Telluride is not a reliable cost comparison for a lot near Norwood. San Miguel County's mountain terrain and variable bedrock make the closest comparable well records more useful than a countywide average.

Colorado DWR records include 3,379 permitted wells across the county, with 1,848 recorded as constructed. The reported median depth is 182 feet and median yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, but those figures come from different subsets of records. Use them to start a budget, then narrow the search to your parcel.

sections.heading: A 182-Foot Median Leaves Plenty of Room in the Bid
sections.html:
Among 2,016 wells reporting depth, the median is 182 feet, and the middle half fall between 75-325 feet. That is a wide enough spread that a flat-price assumption can leave a buyer short. Ask the driller what additional footage costs and how casing and grout are priced if conditions change.

The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet. Most permit aquifer entries are unnamed or classified as fractured bedrock; others name Dakota or Dakota Sandstone. In fractured rock, usable water depends on intersecting connected water-bearing fractures, not simply reaching a uniform underground layer. Compare nearby completion reports around Placerville, Sawpit or Ophir rather than treating every county well as the same drilling job.

sections.heading: What a 7.0 GPM Well Means for a Household
sections.html:
The 717 wells with reported pump yields have a 7.0 gpm median, with the middle half producing 4.0-12.0 gpm. That can support ordinary household use with an appropriately designed system, but a reported test yield is not a guarantee of sustained production through changing conditions.

Low production deserves attention: 4% of reported yields are under 1 gpm, while 21% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. For a buyer, that means checking recovery and peak-demand performance before committing to the property. Storage may help manage intermittent demand, but it cannot create water. Also read the permit: physical production does not establish permission to irrigate or serve additional buildings.

sections.heading: Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Countywide Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the depth to water in a resting well, not the depth of the drilled hole. Across 201 reporting records, the median is 80 feet below ground, with the middle half between 27-183 feet. A pump still needs to be designed around pumping drawdown and the actual well construction.

Median measured levels were 125 feet in the 1990s, 185 feet in the 2000s, 60 feet in the 2010s and 84 feet in the 2020s. That sequence does not establish a steadily dropping countywide water table. These are grouped measurements, not a repeated record from the same wells. Local measurements and pumping history matter more for evaluating a particular property.

sections.heading: The County's Drilling Record Is Heaviest in Earlier Decades
sections.html:
Permit issuance was strongest in the 1990s, with 944 permits, followed by 849 in the 2000s. Records show 308 in the 2010s and 224 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, and permit totals are not the same as completed domestic wells. Monitoring accounts for 22% of the recorded use mix.

The most active drillers in the records are Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.) with 424, Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth) with 399, and Mccracken Well Drilling Inc (Mccracken, Alan E.) with 255. Those counts show historical presence, not current availability. Ask prospective drillers about recent experience near your parcel and comparable ground conditions.

sections.heading: Budget Beyond the Hole in San Miguel County
sections.html:
The supplied cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, such as granite or gneiss, at $65-$100 per foot. At the county's 182-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $11,800-$18,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $17,800-$30,200.

Treat that as a planning allowance, not a parcel-specific quote. The 75-325-foot middle depth range means footage alone can change the job substantially. Mountain access, a workable rig pad, casing requirements and the route to the house also affect the scope. Get a written breakdown showing what is included, what is an allowance and what happens if the initial bore does not produce usable water.

sections.heading: Mine Features, Water Testing and Low-Yield Risk
sections.html:
The supplied environmental mapping lists 1,093 historic mine features, 12 PFAS sampling/contamination sites and 11 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped features are reasons to investigate location and groundwater pathways; they do not establish that a particular well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling site alone does not prove a detection.

Before buying, obtain laboratory water testing and ask the lab or local health authority which additional analyses fit the property's setting. Review casing, grout and the wellhead for sanitary protection. Check production separately from water quality: fractured-bedrock drilling can encounter inadequate water. Place the proposed septic system and building footprint with required well separation, terrain and future service access in mind.

sections.heading: Before Closing on Land Near Norwood or Mountain Village
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit and well completion report. Confirm that the permit belongs to the property, allows the intended uses and matches the existing installation. An exempt household-use permit does not automatically authorize outdoor watering. A proposed use may require a different permitting path or augmentation in an over-appropriated basin.

Then compare nearby wells on similar terrain around Norwood, Mountain Village or the property's actual neighborhood. Do not substitute records from Ouray County or Montrose County merely because they are nearby. For an existing home, review a current production test and laboratory results. For vacant land, coordinate the well location, rig access, driveway, septic area and house site before finalizing the build layout or purchase contingencies.

faq.q: How deep are wells in San Miguel County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth is 182 feet, and the middle half range from 75-325 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet. These figures come from 2,016 depth reports across the county. Fractured bedrock makes depth variable, so nearby completion reports on similar terrain are a better bidding guide than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in San Miguel County?
faq.a: The bedrock drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the median depth of 182 feet, the drilled hole is about $11,800-$18,200, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $17,800-$30,200. Ask for a parcel-specific quote that addresses access, casing, additional footage and the scope of utility connections.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in San Miguel County?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 7.0 gpm, with the middle half at 4.0-12.0 gpm. Among reporting wells, 4% yield under 1 gpm. Before buying, request a production and recovery test rather than relying only on the original drilling report. Household performance depends on sustained supply, storage and demand, not just the pump's capacity.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in San Miguel County?
faq.a: Safety has to be established for the individual well through laboratory testing and inspection. The supplied mapping includes 1,093 historic mine features and 12 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles, but those counts do not establish contamination at your property. Review nearby environmental records and ask which tests are appropriate for the well's location.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in San Miguel County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady decline. Static water depths were 125 feet in the 1990s, 185 in the 2000s, 60 in the 2010s and 84 in the 2020s. These grouped records are not repeat measurements of the same wells. Evaluate local water-level and pumping history before drawing conclusions about a specific property.
